title: Lesson 95 - There Are Trade-offs Either Way

lines.speaker: Owen
lines.text: There are trade-offs either way. If we stop now, we protect staff recovery and avoid another evening commitment, but we learn nothing about more varied groups.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: On the one hand, the four-event process stayed inside its limits. On the other hand, the sample was narrow: thirty-four attendees, one menu format and no group larger than ten.

lines.speaker: Malik
lines.text: Even if another bounded round stayed within twenty extra hours, it would still use time that could support daytime service or planned maintenance.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: That’s true. A second round would solve part of the evidence gap, but it would also ask staff to repeat late work without proving a recurring model.

lines.speaker: Owen
lines.text: What about a monthly service? The main benefit would be a clearer offer for groups and more observations over time.

lines.speaker: Malik
lines.text: The main risk is that a pilot gate becomes a routine expectation. Date-specific consent is easier to protect for four trials than for an open-ended calendar.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: We’re working with limited resources. Priority should be given to reliable daytime service unless evening evidence is strong enough to justify displacing it.

lines.speaker: Owen
lines.text: The question is whether the additional evidence from option B is worth the staff time and opportunity cost.

lines.speaker: Malik
lines.text: For me, it is not yet. The trial showed that a very small model can be controlled; it did not reveal a problem that only another immediate round can answer.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: I agree about timing, although I place more weight on preserving the learning. We should keep the checklist and data structure even if we stop evening events.

lines.speaker: Owen
lines.text: Looking back, what would have happened if we had accepted Noor’s original request for eighteen people on six nights?

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: It would have exceeded the guest, date, duration and menu scope before the trial began. We would not have been testing the approved model.

lines.speaker: Malik
lines.text: If we hadn’t required direct schedule confirmation, a general note might have been mistaken for consent. That explains why the gate mattered; it doesn’t mean anyone would certainly have been forced to work.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: If we had kept the separate welcome table after the long second cleanup, we might have used more staff time in the final two events.

lines.speaker: Owen
lines.text: Those counterfactuals identify useful controls, but they do not prove that every future event would fail without them.

lines.speaker: Malik
lines.text: Exactly. The pressure was shared, while the decisions remained separate. Rosa managed the operating plan, each employee accepted a date, and you owned the framework decision.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: My recommendation is to close the old trial and not approve a standing monthly service. Keep the daytime checklist, and treat any future evening idea as a new proposal.

lines.speaker: Owen
lines.text: That gives up immediate evidence from option B. Is the lost learning acceptable?

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: I think so. We have enough evidence to improve daytime bookings, while the unresolved question is not urgent. New demand or new capacity could justify a fresh review later.

lines.speaker: Malik
lines.text: Then the trade-off is clear: we give up immediate evening expansion and additional data in exchange for predictable recovery, protected daytime capacity and an honest end to the pilot.
